Cyclone Resistant Structures Sectional Committee, CED 57 


FOREWORD 


This Indian Standard (First Revision) was adopted by the Bureau of Indian Standards, after the draft finalized by 
the Cyclone Resistant Structures Sectional Committee had been approved by the Civil Engineering Division 
Council. 


Cyclonic storms form far away from the sea coast and gradually reduce in speed as they approach the seacoast. 
Cyclonic storms generally extend up to about 60 km after striking the coast. Cyclones associated with high speed 
winds followed by heavy rains and accompanied by surges have been causing untold misery to the populace and 
widespread devastation of properties in the coastal belts of India. The frequency of cyclonic storms is more along 
the east coast as compared to the west coast of India. The coastal regions of Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Orissa 
and West Bengal on the east coast and Gujarat on the west coast are cyclone prone. Damage to houses is most 
responsible for loss of life and, thus the need to have a greater emphasis on the safety of houses. The provisions 
given in this standard are intended to reduce the damage to low-rise houses in the event of a cyclone. 


In this standard, low-rise houses are categorized as non-engineered, semi-engineered and engineered on the basis 
of engineering and supervision involved. Non-engineered low-rise houses are houses which are constructed by 
using conventional building materials but made intuitively without carrying out a proper structural design and or 
constructed without adequate control at the site, with respect to both materials used and construction practices 
employed are termed as non-engineered construction. Semi-engineered buildings are those buildings which have 
certain elements structurally designed, such as roof slabs and foundations, but certain elements are those not 
properly designed, such as walls of masonry buildings and in which the supervision may be through engineering 
staff or otherwise. Engineered buildings are those buildings designed by architects and/or engineers and properly 
supervised by engineering staff during construction, such as reinforced concrete and steel-framed buildings. 


This standard provides the guidelines for improving the cyclonic resistance of low-rise houses with respect to 
planning, design and construction aspects. This standard was published in 2004 to provide the national standard 
for the design and construction of cyclone-resistant structures so as to ensure desirable level of safety. In this 
revision, the following major modifications have been incorporated: 


a) Vertical reinforcement detailing has been provided for strengthening the corner and junction of a wall 
along with the figure; 

b) Improvement of structural integrity through providing bands at various levels has been incorporated along 
with the figures; 

c) Guidelines regarding improvement in the steel bracing system have been incorporated with the figure; 

d) Component-wise improvements have been suggested; 

е) Improved drawings and illustrations have been elaborated; and 

f) The title of the standard has been changed from ‘Guidelines for improving the cyclonic resistance of 
low-rise houses and other buildings/structures’ to ‘Guidelines for improving the cyclonic resistance of 
low-rise houses and other buildings'. 


The composition of the Committee responsible for the formulation of this standard is given in Annex B. 


This standard contributes to the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals by especially Goal 9 — ‘Industry, 
innovation and infrastructure: Build resilient infrastructure, promote inclusive and sustainable industrialization 
and foster innovation’. 


For the purpose of deciding whether a particular requirement of this standard is complied with, the final value, 
observed or calculated, expressing the result of a test or analysis, shall be rounded off in accordance with 
IS 2 : 2022 ‘Rules for rounding of numerical values (second revision)’. The number of significant places retained 
in the rounded off value should be the same as that of the specified value in this standard.

IMPROVING THE CYCLONIC RESISTANCE OF LOW RISE 
HOUSES AND OTHER BUILDINGS — GUIDELINES 


( First Revision ) 


1SCOPE 


1.1 This standard provides the guidelines for 
improving the cyclonic resistance of low rise houses 
with respect to planning, design and construction 
aspects. 


1.2 IS 18315 that provides the guidelines for 
estimation of cyclonic factor (K,) is a necessary 
adjunct to this standard. 


2 REFERENCES 


The standards given below contain provisions 
which, through reference in this text, constitute 
provisions of this standard. At the time of 
publication, the editions indicated were valid. All 
standards are subject to revision, and parties to 
agreements based on this standard are encouraged to 
investigate the possibility of applying the most 
recent editions of these standards:

3 PRESSURE AND FORCE 


It is known that higher wind speed occurs during 
cyclones compared to non-cyclonic storms. Further, 
there is a greater degree of turbulence in such storms 
and the probability of occurrence during the lifetime 
of a structure is also large. Therefore, structures are 
subjected to greater risk under cyclonic storms. The 
pressure and forces experienced by the various types 
of buildings and structures shall be computed using 


IS 875 (Part 3) by using various coefficients. The 
coefficients for cyclonic factor (K4) shall be 
calculated as per IS 18315. 


Unless measures have been taken to ensure that 
doors and windows would stay in position during a 
storm, failure of the closing element over the largest 
opening shall be considered for computing the 
percentage opening (permeability) in addition to any 
fully vented openings. 


4 GUIDELINES FOR IMPROVING THE 
CYCLONIC RESISTANCE OF LOW-RISE 
HOUSES 


Generally, low-rise houses are constructed by using 
conventional building materials with or without 
carrying out a proper structural design and site 
control. On the basis of engineering and supervision 
involved, low-rise houses in the cyclonic region are 
classified into the following category: 


a) Non-engineered building; 
b) Semi-engineered building; and 
c) Engineered building. 


The improvement suggested are related to 
pre-construction as well as post-construction. 
Detailed guidelines are also suggested for the 
selection and planning of the site. Component-wise 
improvement measures are provided in Annex A. 


4.1 Guidelines for Non-Engineered Building 


All construction though using conventional building 
materials but made intuitively without carrying out 
a proper structural design or constructed without 
adequate control at the site, with respect to both 
materials used and construction practices employed, 
may generally be termed as  non-engineered 
construction. АП construction in low-strength 
masonry or clay mud and similar other forms of 
biomass with fall under the category of non- 
engineered construction. The major chunk of non- 
engineered low rise houses is kutcha houses. 
Guidelines for improving the cyclonic resistance of 
kutcha houses are given in IS 18153. The measures 
suggested here in enhance the cyclonic wind 
resistance to significantly higher levels but still 
lower than  semi-engineered and engineered 
buildings.

The aerodynamics of flow around buildings 
leads to large suction pressures on the roof. 
To reduce problems due to flying-off of 
thatched roof, it may be held down to the 
framework of the roof or the building 
envelope using organic ropes. As organic 
ropes have short life, the holding down ropes 
alone may be changed every year prior to the 
most probable month of occurrence of 
cyclones. Diagonal pattern of rope 18 
preferred (see Fig. 1). 


The overhang of the roof beyond the wall 
shall be limited to 450 mm. Іп case it 
exceeds this value, the projected portion of 
the roof may be properly tied back to the 
wall framework. 


All the posts buried below ground level shall 
be painted with a coat of coal tar up to the 
level of maximum flood discharge. 


The main posts shall be firmly anchored to 
the ground using suitable anchor poles. The 
minimum depth of anchorage for the main 
posts shall be 900 mm, and the minimum 
length of anchorage bars shall be 450 mm, 
with a minimum bearing area of 
22 500 mm?. Each post shall have four 
anchor poles, as shown in Fig. 2 at two 
levels at least at 500 mm intervals in 
different directions. 


As mud wall is erodible, protection barrier 
or revetment built with stone or brick shall 
be built up to the maximum flood level, and 
plastering with special waterproof clay or 
cement/lime mortar on the outer surface is 
essential (see Fig. 3). 


In case of a sloped roof, triangular frames as 
shown in Fig. 4 may be located with a 
maximum spacing of 2.0 m. The members 
of this triangular frame shall be sufficiently

strong to hold back the cross runners. 
Suitable connections shall be ensured 
between various elements of this frame 
using metal straps, bolts and nuts, and steel 
flats to enable better integrity for the 
structure as a whole (see Fig. 5 and Fig. 6). 


The main triangular frames are to be firmly 
connected to anchorage elements/bond 
beams at the level of the eaves. The 
anchorage elements, in turn are to be 
connected to the main posts ofthe wall using 
U-bolts. 


Brickwork in weak mortars and random 
rubble masonry can be used for the walls. In 
these cases, the bond beam/anchorage beam 
provided on top shall be anchored to the 
foundation using a mild steel rod properly 
encased in cement mortar. Alternatively, if 
a continuous lintel is provided with 
reinforced concrete or wood with a 
sufficient height of brick world rubble 
masonry, the roof can be anchored to the 
continuous lintel. The total downward load 
due to the weight of the masonry and roof 
shall have a factor of 1.50 over the total 
uplift force on the roof. The total area of 
anchorage reinforcement provided shall be 
twice that required for transmitting the uplift 
force. 


Discrete anchorage of the roof into 
brick/rubble masonry can be accomplished 
through anchorage reinforcement. An angle 
of dispersion of two verticals to one 
horizontal may be assumed. The shear 
strength of masonry shall be neglected in 
any computation, and the effective weight of 
masonry above shall be 1.5 times the uplift 
force at the given anchorage based on 
simplified load-flow pattern.

4.2 Guidelines for Semi-Engineered Buildings 


Semi-engineered buildings are buildings which have 
certain elements structurally designed, such as roof 
slabs and foundations, but certain elements are not 
properly designed, such as walls of masonry 
buildings and in which the supervision may be 


through Engineering staff or otherwise. 


The 


following guidelines are useful in detailing semi- 
engineered buildings: 


a) 


b) 


c) 


d) 


To achieve a certain measure of restraint 
for tiled roofs, provide concrete or masonry 
restraining bands at a spacing of 
approximately 1.2 m to 1.5 m. These bands 
may preferably be located over wooden 
rafters forming an integral part of the truss 
system. In case the bands are connected to 
the purlins, U-bolts may be used and 
suitably anchored over the reinforcing rod. 
The dimension of the band may be about 
100 mm x 50 mm. The restraining bands 
shall have at least on 10 mm diameter bar 
placed inside the band. Typical details of 
improvements to tiled roof are given in Fig. 
7. Hip, valley and ridge tiles shall be firmly 
embedded in continuous band of cement 
mortar. If nailing holes are available in 
these tiles, nails can be inserted through 
these into the mortar bed and these can 
effectively serve as shear connectors. 


The tiled roof system shall be securely fixed 
to a bond beam. The bond beam in turn is to 
be connected to the foundation by holding 
down bolts. The holding down bolt shall be 
designed with a factor of safety of 2.0. 


Wherever asbestos sheets are used for roof 
cladding, U-bolts are preferred when 
compared to J-bolts. The numbers of 
U-bolts at various locations are indicated 
in Fig. 8. 


In case hollow concrete block masonry is 
used for walls, the designed reinforcements 
can be taken through the hollow concrete 


e) 


8) 


block forming a pilaster with reinforcement 
as shown in Fig. 9. The spacing of such 
pilasters shall not be greater than 3.0 m. 
The reinforcements are to be anchored well 
into the foundation and integrated with 
lintel band and bond beam (see Fig. 10). 


Good connections are required among the 
various wooden elements in the roof and 
wall. Typical details shown in Fig. 11 and 
Fig. 12 may be adopted with modifications 
to suit the structural scheme. Тһе 
important requirement is that the uplift 
force on the roof is to be safely transmitted 
to the foundation. The connections must 
have adequate strength to transfer the uplift 
force. 


If a strong wall made of good quality 
brickwork is provided, the roof can be 
anchored to the continuous lintel band 


through cyclone bolts. 
Vertical | reinforcement at corners, 
junctions of walls — Тһе vertical 


reinforcement consisting of 12 mm HSD 
bar or equivalent shall be provided on the 
inside corner (Fig. 13) of room starting 
from 750 mm below the ground floor going 
up to the roof. The reinforcement shall be 
connected to the walls by using L-shaped 
dowels of 8 mm TOR Баг, the vertical leg 
of 400 mm length firmly tied to the vertical 
reinforcement bars and the horizontal leg of 
minimum 150 mm length embedded in the 
walls through 75 mm diameter holes drilled 
in the wall into which the 8 mm diameter 
leg of the dowel will be grouted using non- 
shrink cement cum polymer grout. Such 
dowels will be provided, first just above 
plinth level and then at about every 1 m 
distance apart. The corner reinforcement 
will be covered with 1 : 3 cement mortar or 
1:1.5:3 micro concrete fully bonded with 
the walls giving minimum cover of 15 mm 
on the bar.

h) Strengthening of walls during construction 


against high winds/cyclones — For high 
wind and cyclone prone areas (Vy > 50 m/s), 
it 1s found necessary to use 1 : 4 cement, 
sand-mortar in construction of masonry 
walls. Reinforced concrete (RC) bands 
should be provided to reinforce the walls at 
the door-window lintel level, eaves level of 
pitched roofs, below flexible flat roofs, and 
on top of external gable walls. Lintel band 
is a band provided at lintel level on all load 
bearing internal, external longitudinal and 
cross walls. Roof band or eave band is a 
band provided immediately below the roof 
or floors. Such a band need not be provided 
underneath reinforced concrete or brick- 
work Slabs resting on bearing walls 
provided that the slabs are continuous over 
the intermediate wall. Gable band 18 a band 


provided at the top of gable masonry below 
the purlins. This band shall be made 
continuous with the roof band at the eaves 
level. The band shall be made of reinforced 
concrete of grade not less than M20. Band 
should be covering the width of end walls, 
fully or at least 3/4 of the wall thickness, as 
shown in Fig. 14. The section and 
reinforcement details of band are given in 
Table 1. The following should be 
considered while providing the RC band: 


1) Span of wall will be the distance 
between centre lines of its cross walls or 
buttresses. For spans greater than 8 m, it 
will be desirable to insert pilasters or 
buttresses to reduce the span. 


2) Width of RC band is assumed to be the 
same as the thickness of the wall. Wall

4.3 Guidelines for Improving the Design of 
Engineered Buildings 


Engineered buildings are buildings designed by 
architects and/or engineers and properly supervised 
by engineering staff during construction, such as, 
reinforced concrete and steel framed buildings. 
Public buildings, such as, schools and hospitals, 
cyclone shelters, etc have to be carefully engineered. 


a) Ina cluster of buildings having similar heights 
and where the inter-building spacing is less 
than 2 times the width of an individual 
building, the following enhancement/shielding 
factors are to be considered. 


1) For corner buildings located on the 
periphery of the building clusters, the 
pressure loadings shall be enhanced by 
a factor of 1.50. 

2) For all interior buildings, a shielding 
factor of 0.80 can be considered. 

3) The roof pressures on corner buildings 
of the outer rows shall be enhanced by 
a factor of 1.50 in industrial sheds. 

4) For evaluating the roof pressures on 
interior buildings, a shielding factor of 
0.80 can be considered for gabled roofs. 


b) In all buildings where wind loading is the 
dominant loading no increase in allowable 
stresses in steel over and above that 
specified in IS 800 is permitted. 


c) In ай buildings where load bearing 
masonry is used, a parapet of minimum 
height of 600 mm may be provided. Also 
the roof slab may be anchored to the 
continuous lintel through adequate ties. 


d) In  multü-hazard prone areas with 
earthquake zone III and above, even if the 
design forces are governed by wind 
loading, ductile detailing provisions as 
given in IS 13920 shall be followed. The 
design forces would however be computed 
based on wind loading in such cases. 


е) In flood prone areas, all public buildings 
including cyclone shelters, shall be 
constructed оп raised ground with 
appropriate peripheral retaining walls. 


f) If buildings are constructed with openings 
at the ground level/stilled buildings, 
adequate symmetric shear walls shall be 
provided in both the principal directions of 


IS 15498 : 2023 


buildings. This is absolutely essential in 
multi-hazard prone areas for earthquake 
regions with zone III and above. 


g) Wherever feasible, without compromising 
functionality, the comers of the buildings 
shall be rounded off with suitable radius of 
curvature so as to reduce the drag forces. 


h) In industrial buildings with gable roofs, 
plan bracing shall invariably be provided at 
the bottom chord level of trusses to avoid 
bottom chord buckling due to uplift forces 
as well as to distribute the horizontal 
loading from gable ends (see Fig. 15). 
Upper chord bracing is also desirable at 
least near gable end walls. 


1) In steel bracing system, adequate diagonal 
or knee bracing should be provided both at 
the rafter level and the eaves level in a 
pitched roof. Тһе purlins should be 
properly anchored at the gable end. It 1s 
desirable that at least two bays, one at each 
end, be braced both in horizontal and 
vertical planes to provide adequate wind 
resistance. Where number of bays is more 
than 5, use additional bracing in every 
fourth bay. In order to reduce wind induced 
flutter/vibration of the roof in cyclonic 
regions, it is recommended that all 
members of the truss and the bracings be 
connected at the ends by at least two bolts 
or welds. Further, the cross-bracing 
members are welded/connected at the 
crossings to reduce vibrations (see Fig. 16 
and Fig. 17). 


4.4 Guidelines Related to Selection and Planning 


Though cyclonic storms always approach from the 
direction of the sea towards the coast, the wind 
velocity and direction relative to a building remain 
random. Hence, reduction coefficients for 
directionality and orientation. of buildings in a 
preferential direction are not feasible. The general 
guidelines for planning include the following: 


a) As far as possible, the building shall be 
founded on good ground. Part of the 
building on good ground and partly on made 
up ground shall be avoided (see Fig. 18). 


b) Regular plan shapes are preferred. Re- 
entrant corners are to Бе avoided 
(see Fig. 19).

FIG. 19 SUGGESTED IMPROVEMENT FOR BUILDING PLANS 


For individual buildings, a circular or 
polygonal plan is preferred over rectangular 
or square plans but from the view point of 
functional efficiency, often a rectangular 
plan is commonly used. Where most 
prevalent wind direction is known, a 
building should be so oriented, where 
feasible, that its smallest facade face the 
wind. 


A symmetrical building with a compact plan 
form is more stable than an asymmetrical 
building with a zig-zag plan, having empty 
pockets as the latter is more prone to 
wind/cyclone related damage (see Fig. 20). 


In case of the construction of group of 
buildings with a row type or cluster 
arrangement, cluster arrangement can be 
followed in preference to row type. 
However, in certain cases, both may give 
rise to adverse wind pressure due to tunnel 
action and studies need to be conducted to 


МУ 


8 


h) 


j 


look into this aspect (see Fig. 21). 


Long walls having length more than 3.5 m 
shall be provided with cross walls or 
integrated pilasters (see Fig. 22). 


In hilly regions, construction along ridges 
should be avoided since they experience an 
accentuation of wind velocity, whereas 
valleys experience lower speeds in general 
(see Fig. 23). 


Except in case of buildings with large spans 
with sloped roofs, roof pitches having a 
slope less than 1 in 3 shall be avoided 
(see Fig. 24). 


Hipped roofs are preferred to gabled roofs 
for non-engineered and semi-engineered 
buildings as the peak suction pressures for 
all angles of attack are lower in the former 
case and may be taken as 80 percent of those 
on pitched gabled roofs in the absence of 
more detailed information (see Fig. 25). 


IS 15498 : 2023 


k) 


m) 


The percent of the total opening in the cross 
section of the frontal wall shall be less than 
50 percent of the width of the wall, opening 
in load bearing walls should not be within 
a distance of h/6 from the inner corner for 
the purpose of providing lateral support to 
cross walls, where the storey height up to 
eave level (see Fig. 26). 


While planning a layout for group housing, 
if the inter-building spacing is less than 
twice the width of the building, 
considerable shielding is available for the 
interior buildings though the first two 
columns show attracting larger forces 
compared to a stand-alone building. 


n) In regions where storm surges lead 


to coastal inundation, buildings 
should be located at higher ground 
levels. If high ground is not available, 
buildings may Бе constructed at 
raised earthen mounds suitably 
surrounded Бу retaining walls. 
Alternatively, buildings may 
be constructed with stilts with no 
masonry up to maximum surge level. 
Suitable bracings may, however, be 
provided in case of multiple hazard 
zones, particularly due to earthquakes, 
to avoid failures arising out of large 
variations in stiffness between stilt and 
higher floor levels.

ANNEX A 
(Clause 4) 
BUILDING COMPONENT WISE IMPROVEMENT MEASURES 


SI No. Component Material of Improvement Measure 
Construction 
(1) (2) (3) (4) 
1) Foundation a) The entire foundation of a house should be 
constructed on the same soil and not on made-up 
soil. 


b) Each vertical post of wall should be buried in at 
least M20 grade concrete up to 900 mm depth 
from ground level. 


ii) Wall a) Provide a continuous reinforcement concrete 
cement bond beam over the walls to improve the 
lateral resistance of the supporting brick walls. 


b) The length of an individual wall should be kept 
than 3.5 m (127) which can be achieved by 
provision of intervening cross walls or pilasters. 


iii) Wall framing Balli/bamboo wall Diagonal bracing system and vertical support should 
framing be used to strengthen the walls. 
Timber wall a) J-shaped anchors should be embedded into the 
concrete for fixing the timber walls with the 
foundation. 


b) ISA 50 mm х 50 mm х 3 mm or MS plate of size 
(3 х 25)mm and 15 mm long nails/screws should 
be used as connectors for connecting the members 
of wall frame. 


c) Vertical posts, roofs and walls must be braced tied 
with 50 mm long screws in each direction. 


Masonry wall a) Theopening near to the edge of the wall should be 
positioned with a minimum distance of 600 mm. 


b) The vertical reinforcement consisting of 12 mm 
bar or equivalent shall be provided on the inside 
corner. 


iv) Verandah Wide mono-pitched verandas abutting the entrance to 
residence should be structurally separated from the 
main building. 


v) Projection Projections should be avoided to the extent possible, 
(chajja) and closed configuration (square/rectangle) should be 
adopted for house plans.

Sheeted roof 


а) A hip-shaped, pyramidal or conical roofing be 
preferred to gable end or mono-pitch ones. 


b) The overhang at eaves shall not exceed 450 mm. 
In case it exceeds this value, the projected portion 
of the roof may be properly tied back to the wall 
frame work. 


c) Eavelevel bracing may be provided under the roof 
framing and additional diagonal “Х” bracing on 
roof level. 


d) Provide suitable bracing of the roofing system to 
avoid progressive collapse of the roof-truss 
system. 


e) For roof cladding, we should provide additional 
numbers of U-bolts at ridges and eaves. 


f) Roof structures shall be properly secured with 
vertical load-bearing members for eliminating the 
chances of being blown away from the building. 


Roof cladding be properly connected by holding down 
U-bolts or sturdy anchorages to ensure safety. 


Thatched roofs should be properly tied down to 
wooden framing underneath by using organic or nylon 
ropes in diagonal patterns. 


Anchoring of roof tiles ш RC strap beams 18 
recommended for improved cyclone resistance. 


Spaces between the sheeting and the wall plate should 
be closed up to prevent the wind from getting under 
the sheeting and lifting it. 


a) Door or window frames be securely fixed in the 
walls using holdfasts so as to resist the local wind 
pressures. 


b) Use strong wide tapes or wooden battens for 
windows. 


a) Glass panels can be strengthened by pasting thin 
plastic film or paper strips. 


b) To prevent damage to the glass panels from flying 
wind-borne missiles, a metallic fabric/mesh 
should be provided outside the large panels. 

c) Protection of glass paneling and adequate 


anchorage of wooden door and window frames 
with holdfasts.

Bureau of Indian Standards 


BIS is a statutory institution established under the Bureau of Indian Standards Act, 2016 to promote harmonious 
development of the activities of standardization, marking and quality certification of goods and attending to 
connected matters in the country. 


Copyright 


BIS has the copyright of all its publications. No part of these publications may be reproduced in any form without 
the prior permission in writing of BIS. This does not preclude the free use, in the course of implementing the 
standard, of necessary details, such as symbols and sizes, type or grade designations. Enquiries relating to 
copyright be addressed to the Head (Publication & Sales), BIS. 


Review of Indian Standards 


Amendments are issued to standards as the need arises on the basis of comments. Standards are also reviewed 
periodically; a standard along with amendments is reaffirmed when such review indicates that no changes are 
needed; if the review indicates that changes are needed, it is taken up for revision. Users of Indian Standards 
should ascertain that they are in possession of the latest amendments or edition by referring to the 
website- www.bis.gov.in or www.standardsbis.in. 


This Indian Standard has been developed from Doc No.:CED 57 (21877).
